howItWorks.intro: This calculator adds up three night categories at three different price points, because lumping every campground night into one flat average hides where your money is actually going on a mixed-route RV trip.

rules.name: Blended Campground Cost
rules.formula: Total = (Private Resort Nights × $65) + (Public/State Park Nights × $28) + (Free Nights × $0)
rules.explanation: $65 reflects a typical full-hookup site (water, sewer, 30/50-amp power) at a private RV resort or KOA-style park; $28 reflects a typical electric-and-water site at a state, county, or Army Corps park without sewer. Free nights cover BLM dispersed camping, Harvest Hosts stops, and overnight lots, which carry no site fee but usually mean no hookups at all.

howItWorks.outro: Your actual rates will move with season, region, and site type — a 50-amp pull-through on the California coast in July costs more than a 30-amp back-in site in rural Kansas in October. Treat the total here as a planning budget, then swap in real rates once you've picked actual campgrounds and checked their current pricing.

faq.question: How much do RV campgrounds actually cost per night?
faq.answer: State and county parks with electric and water run about $20-40/night depending on region. Private RV resorts and KOA-style parks with full hookups (water, sewer, 30/50-amp power) typically run $50-100+/night, with national-park-adjacent locations and holiday weekends pushing toward the top of that range. Free options — BLM dispersed land, Harvest Hosts stops, some Walmart and Cracker Barrel lots — have no site fee but almost never include hookups.

faq.question: Is a camping membership like Good Sam or Thousand Trails worth it?
faq.answer: It depends on how many nights you'll actually spend at member parks. Good Sam's roughly 10% discount on a $65 private-park night saves about $6.50 — nice if you stay at Good Sam parks often, but not enough alone to justify a detour. Thousand Trails' annual zone pass (around $500-600) can pay for itself in 8-10 nights at parks that would otherwise run $60-70, which makes it worthwhile mainly for snowbirds and full-timers logging 3+ weeks at member parks in a year. Harvest Hosts (about $99/year) trades free overnight parking at wineries, farms, and breweries for the expectation you'll buy something from the host — cheap insurance against a string of expensive private-park nights on a long haul.

faq.question: What's the real difference between 30-amp and 50-amp hookups?
faq.answer: A 30-amp site tops out around 3,600 watts — fine for one AC unit, the fridge, and basic electronics, but it'll trip the breaker if you run a second AC and the microwave at once. A 50-amp site actually provides two separate 50-amp legs (close to 12,000 watts total) for bigger rigs running multiple AC units, electric water heaters, and residential appliances. Public parks lean 30-amp or electric-only; private resorts almost always offer 50-amp, which is part of why their rates run higher.

faq.question: What other costs should I add to my nightly campground budget?
faq.answer: Dump fees ($10-20 per use) if you're dry camping between paid stops, propane (roughly $15-20 per 20-lb tank fill, lasting 1-2 weeks for cooking and furnace use), and reservation deposits — usually 1-2 nights' rate, charged when you book and often non-refundable inside 7-14 days of arrival. On a multi-week trip, budget an extra 10-15% on top of your raw nightly total to cover these.

faq.question: How do I budget campground costs for a 2+ week trip?
faq.answer: Mix your nights deliberately instead of defaulting to private resorts everywhere. For example, 14 nights split 8 at state parks ($28) and 6 at private resorts ($65) totals $224 + $390 = $614, or about $44/night average. Apply a 10% Good Sam discount to the 6 private nights and you save roughly $39, bringing the trip to about $575. Run your own split through the calculator above to see how shifting even two or three nights from resort to state park moves your total.

howWeCalculate.intro: The math is simple addition, but getting a number you can trust means being honest about which nights fall into which bucket before you start.
steps: Count your planned nights by type — full-hookup private resort, electric/water public park, and free or dry-camping nights — instead of guessing one flat rate for the whole trip.
The calculator multiplies each category by its typical rate and adds them together, the same way you'd total a stack of campground receipts after the fact.
It also divides the total by your overall night count to give you a true blended average per night, which is usually different from whatever single number you had in your head.
Compare that average against your planned daily budget — including propane, fuel, and food — to see whether the lodging side of the trip is the part that actually needs adjusting.
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: These are planning estimates built on typical current rates. Actual site fees vary by park, season, and whether you book direct or through a membership network, so check the specific campground's posted rate before you reserve.

whenToUse.intro: Reach for this before you book anything, and again whenever the route changes.
scenarios: You're mapping a multi-week route and want to know whether leaning on state parks over private resorts actually saves meaningful money, not just a few dollars a night.
You're deciding if a Thousand Trails or Good Sam membership is worth the annual fee for the specific mix of nights your trip will actually use.
You're comparing a national-park-adjacent loop with resort-priced gateway towns against a quieter backroads route with cheaper public camping.
You're building a trip budget that needs a defensible campground number before you commit to reservation deposits, which are often non-refundable past a cutoff date.
You've already booked some nights and want to see how much room is left in the budget for the nights you haven't locked in yet.

sections.title: What Is the RV Campground Budget Calculator?
sections.body: Campground costs are the one expense on an RV trip that swings the hardest depending on where you park at night. A state park site with just electric and water might run $28, while a full-hookup spot at a private resort chain can hit $65 to $100+ once you add a premium pull-through or a holiday-weekend surcharge. This calculator splits your trip into private resort nights, public/state park nights, and free nights (BLM land, Harvest Hosts, Walmart lots, or boondocking) so you can see the real blended cost before you ever leave the driveway. Enter how many nights fall into each category and it adds them up into a total budget and a true average cost per night — the number that actually matters when you're comparing a fast interstate route against a slower one with more state park stops along the way.

sections.title: Why This Calculation Matters
sections.body: Campground fees are usually the single biggest recurring line item on an RV trip, often bigger than fuel once you're not logging serious mileage every day. A quick mental average can mislead you here: plan on "$40 a night" and then discover your actual route puts you in $65 resorts near national parks half the time, because that's where the available sites are, and your real average lands closer to $46 — a gap that adds up fast over two or three weeks. A 50-amp full-hookup site, a 30-amp partial-hookup site, and a dry-camping spot with no hookups at all aren't interchangeable; they carry different rates and different limits on how long you can stay before you need a dump and fresh water. Running the actual mix of nights through real numbers, instead of eyeballing an average, is what keeps a three-week loop from outrunning what you set aside for it.

sections.title: When Should You Use This Calculator?
sections.body: Use it while you're still building the route, before any deposits go down. It's the right tool for deciding between a park-heavy itinerary — more scenery, lower nightly rates, but 30/50-amp availability can be hit or miss — and a resort-heavy one that guarantees full hookups, a pool, and laundry at close to double the cost. It's also useful once you're weighing a membership: Thousand Trails, Good Sam, Escapees, or an annual Harvest Hosts pass. Each one only pays off against your specific night mix, not in the abstract, so running your actual itinerary through the math beats guessing. Try it once with your planned split, then again after shifting a few nights between categories, to see how much that change really moves the total.

howToSteps.title: Split Your Trip Into Night Types
howToSteps.description: Go through your route and tag each planned night as private resort (full hookup), public/state park (partial hookup), or free/dry camping — this is the step that actually determines your budget, more than any single rate does.

howToSteps.title: Enter Your Night Counts
howToSteps.description: Fill in total nights, then how many fall into private parks, public parks, and free camping. The three category counts should add up to your total nights.

howToSteps.title: Calculate Your Blended Budget
howToSteps.description: Click Calculate to see your total campground cost and your true average per night across the whole trip, blending the cheap nights with the expensive ones.

howToSteps.title: Adjust For Your Actual Bookings
howToSteps.description: Once you have real reservations, swap in actual rates for the categories where you know them and re-run the numbers to tighten the estimate before the trip.

tips: Book shoulder-season weeks (May, September, early October) when you can — the same full-hookup site that runs $85 over a July holiday weekend often drops to $55-60 in late September.

A Thousand Trails zone pass runs roughly $500-600/year and makes member parks effectively free after the first few weeks of use, but it only pays off if your route actually passes through zone parks, so check their map against your itinerary before you buy one.
Factor in dump fees ($10-20 per use) for any dry-camping or free nights where you're not hooked up to sewer — they add up fast across a week of boondocking between paid stops.

Reservation deposits at popular private parks usually run 1-2 nights' rate and go non-refundable inside 7-14 days of arrival, so only lock in dates you're confident about before you count that money as still flexible.

A 20-lb propane tank (roughly $15-20 to fill) typically covers 1-2 weeks of cooking and furnace use for a couple in mild weather — plan on double that for cold-weather trips where the furnace runs overnight.
